title: Pinocchio meets the Fox and the Cat again and goes with them to plant the four coins in the Field of Miracles.
paragraphs: As you can imagine, the Fairy let the puppet cry and howl for a good half-hour over his nose, which no longer fitted through the bedroom door: and she did this to teach him a firm lesson and cure him of the nasty habit of telling lies, the nastiest habit a child can have. But when she saw his face changed and his eyes bulging with despair, she took pity on him and clapped her hands, and at that signal a thousand large birds called Woodpeckers flew through the window into the room, and, landing all over Pinocchio’s nose, they pecked and pecked at it until, in a few minutes, that huge, ridiculous nose was back to its normal size.
“How kind you are, my Fairy,” said the puppet, wiping his eyes, “and how much I love you!”
“I love you too,” replied the Fairy, “and if you want to stay with me, you will be my little brother and I will be your kind little sister…”
“I’d love to stay… but what about my poor father?”
“I’ve thought of everything. Your father has already been told: and before nightfall he will be here.”
“Really?” cried Pinocchio, jumping for joy. “Then, my dear Fairy, if you don’t mind, I’d like to go and meet him! I can’t wait to kiss that poor old man who has suffered so much because of me!”
“Go ahead, but take care not to get lost. Take the path through the wood, and I’m sure you’ll meet him.”

Pinocchio set off: and as soon as he entered the wood, he began running like a deer. But when he reached a certain spot, almost opposite the Great Oak, he stopped, because he thought he had heard people among the branches. And there on the road appeared, guess who?… the Fox and the Cat, the two travelling companions with whom he had eaten supper at the Red Crayfish Inn.
“Here is our dear Pinocchio!” cried the Fox, hugging and kissing him. “How come you’re here?”
“How come you’re here?” repeated the Cat.
“It’s a long story,” said the puppet, “and I’ll tell you when there’s time. But you should know that the other night, when you left me alone at the inn, I met murderers on the road…”
“Murderers? Oh, our poor friend! And what did they want?”
“They wanted to steal my gold coins.”
“Villains!” said the Fox.
“Terrible villains!” repeated the Cat.
“But I began to run away,” the puppet went on, “and they kept chasing me: until they caught me and hanged me from a branch of that oak…”
And Pinocchio pointed to the Great Oak, which stood just a few steps away.
“Could anything be worse?” said the Fox. “What a world we are forced to live in! Where can honest folk like us find a safe place?”
While they were talking like this, Pinocchio noticed that the Cat was limping on his right front leg because the whole paw and its claws were missing; so he asked:
“What have you done with your paw?”
The Cat wanted to answer something, but got muddled. Then the Fox said at once:

“My friend is too modest, and that is why he doesn’t answer. I’ll answer for him. You see, an hour ago we met an old wolf on the road, almost fainting with hunger, who asked us for something to eat. Since we didn’t have even a fishbone to give him, what did my friend, who truly has a heart as generous as Caesar’s, do? He bit off a paw from one of his front legs and threw it to that poor creature, so he could have a meal.”
And as the Fox said this, he wiped away a tear.
Pinocchio, moved as well, went up to the Cat and whispered in his ear:
“If all cats were like you, how lucky mice would be!”
“And what are you doing here now?” the Fox asked the puppet.
“I’m waiting for my father, who should arrive here at any moment.”
“And your gold coins?”
“They’re still in my pocket, except for one I spent at the Red Crayfish Inn.”
“And to think that instead of four coins, they could be a thousand or two thousand tomorrow! Why don’t you take my advice? Why don’t you go and plant them in the Field of Miracles?”
“I can’t today: I’ll go another day.”
“Another day will be too late!” said the Fox.
“Why?”
“Because that field has been bought by a rich gentleman, and from tomorrow onwards no one will be allowed to plant money there any more.”
“How far is the Field of Miracles from here?”

“Only two kilometres. Will you come with us? You’ll be there in half an hour: you plant the four coins straight away: after a few minutes you collect two thousand, and this evening you come back here with your pockets full. Will you come with us?”

Pinocchio hesitated a little before answering, because he remembered the good Fairy, old Geppetto and the Talking Cricket’s warnings; but in the end he did what all children with no sense and no heart do; that is, he gave his head a little shake and said to the Fox and the Cat:
“Let’s go; I’ll come with you.”
And they set off.

After walking for half a day, they reached a town called “Foolcatcher.” As soon as he entered the town, Pinocchio saw all the streets filled with dogs with patchy fur yawning with hunger, sheep with their wool cut off trembling with cold, hens without combs or wattles begging for a grain of corn, large butterflies that could no longer fly because they had sold their beautiful coloured wings, peacocks with no tails who were ashamed to show themselves, and pheasants creeping quietly along, mourning their shining gold and silver feathers, now lost for ever.
Among this crowd of beggars and ashamed poor creatures, fine carriages passed from time to time, carrying a Fox, a thieving Magpie or some ugly bird of prey.
“And where is the Field of Miracles?” asked Pinocchio.
“Just a few steps from here.”
No sooner said than done, they crossed the town and, going outside its walls, stopped in an empty field that looked more or less like any other field.
“Here we are,” the Fox said to the puppet. “Now bend down, dig a little hole in the field with your hands, and put the gold coins in it.”
Pinocchio obeyed. He dug the hole, put in the four gold coins he had left, and then covered the hole with a little earth.
“Now,” said the Fox, “go to the water channel nearby, fetch a bucket of water and water the ground where you have planted them.”
Pinocchio went to the water channel and, because he had no bucket handy, took a slipper off his foot, filled it with water and watered the earth covering the hole. Then he asked:
“Is there anything else to do?”
“Nothing else,” replied the Fox. “Now we can leave. You come back here in about twenty minutes, and you’ll find the little tree already growing out of the ground, with its branches covered in coins.”
The poor puppet, beside himself with joy, thanked the Fox and the Cat a thousand times and promised them a wonderful present.
“We don’t want presents,” replied the two scoundrels. “It is enough for us to have taught you how to become rich without any hard work, and we couldn’t be happier.”
Having said this, they said goodbye to Pinocchio, wished him a good harvest and went about their business.
